AI isn't the hard part anymore. Getting it to understand your business is.

For advertising analytics, that means the attribution model. Ads > CRM > revenue. Your definition of a qualified lead. Your view on what's brand vs. what's demand.

We've spent years building those models for clients. This week we shipped a way to access them directly in Claude: the Outshine MCP.

A client can open Claude and ask "Q1 pipeline from competitor search, excluding EMEA" and get an answer from their own attribution model.

Runs inside Looker's governed semantic layer, built on the attribution model we've shaped for each client. 

In beta with clients now.

You’d be getting someone who can absolutely demolish the expectations you have of what is possible in 12 months.

So… throwing it out there. I am extremely confident in what he can do and I’ve referred him successfully before. 

I profit nothing off of this recommendation except maybe a nice gift basket if he takes your gig, so there's no monetary incentive for me to pass his name along. I just think he's great.

Deal Tags are one the most underrated feature in HubSpot Deal tags can completely change how you manage your deal pipeline. They’re color labels that flag what matters in your pipeline: High-value deals, stalled deals, or missing info — right on your deal board. Set them up in Settings → Objects → Deals → Pipelines → Deal Tags. Give each tag a name, color, and rule. For example, tag deals over €50,000 as “High Value,” or deals with no activity for 30 days as “Stale.” HubSpot applies and removes tags automatically as conditions change. Here’s a simple structure to keep it clear: 1. Activity (Needs Follow-Up, Stale) 2. Data (Missing Info) 3. Value (Large Deal) 4. Type (Renewal, Expansion) Keep it simple — 6–8 tags max. Use clear names and distinct colors so everyone instantly understands what each tag means. The real benefit isn’t the colors, it’s the focus. Deal Tags make it easier for sales reps to act fast and for managers to spot issues before they snowball.

Start showing up exactly where they already are: even if that's at your competitor's front door. Geo-fencing isn't just a buzzword. It's a precision-guided strategy that lets you drop a digital perimeter around specific locations. When your target audience walks in, your brand walks in with them. Marketing has become obsessed with what’s measurable. Clicks. Views. CTR. CPM. But most buying decisions aren’t made because someone clicked an ad once. They’re made because the brand felt familiar when it mattered. Memory drives decisions more than metrics. That’s why some brands convert better even with worse ads. They’ve already earned a place in the customer’s mind before the moment of action. DOOH plays a role social can’t fully replicate; It creates memory without requiring engagement. You don’t need to click it. You don’t need to like it. You just need to see it… repeatedly. The brands that win aren’t the ones chasing the cleanest dashboards. They’re the ones building familiarity and trust long before the sale. #MarketingStrategy #BrandBuilding #DOOH #DigitalOutOfHome #Advertising #BrandAwareness

Investors are cautious. Budgets are tight. Every hire has to carry real weight from day one. Founders can't afford the ramp time. They can't afford the learning curve. They need someone who's already done the work outbound, cold calls, territory development, revenue generation. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀: Your narrative needs to shift from "I can do this" to "I've done this." That doesn't mean you hire the most experienced person. It means you hire someone with recent, relevant proof. They've shipped product in the last 12 months. They've closed deals in the last quarter. They've built a team, process, or system that's still working today. Not five years ago at a different company in a different market. Recently. Because the market has changed. The playbooks have changed. And what worked in 2021 doesn't work now. Founders who are still hiring for potential are getting burned. The ones who are hiring for proof are building teams that can actually execute. There's no room for passengers anymore. Is this too harsh, or just the reality?
